key_facts: The **red leg** is a common diagnostic trap: most bilateral red legs are **not cellulitis**.
Cellulitis is usually **unilateral**, acute, hot, tender, spreading, with fever or raised inflammatory markers.
Mimics: venous (stasis) eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, contact dermatitis, DVT, haematoma, gout, erythema nodosum, vasculitis.
Bilateral red legs: treat the cause (compression, emollient, steroid for eczema); avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
Same-day: sepsis, rapidly spreading, severe pain out of proportion (necrotising fasciitis), suspected DVT.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: ‘Red leg’ is a presentation, not a diagnosis. Up to a third of patients admitted with ‘cellulitis’ turn out to have a **mimic** (pseudocellulitis). This page brings together the Module 5 red-leg teaching and the referral triggers for leg ulcers.

sub: Up to a third of patients admitted with 'cellulitis' have a mimic, often stasis dermatitis.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Different processes make legs red: **infection, venous hypertension, allergy, thrombosis or inflammation**.

mech.t: Stasis causes oedema, inflammation and eczema (bilateral, itchy, chronic).
Bacteria enter via breaks (tinea, ulcers) and spread through dermis and fat (unilateral, acute).
Dressings and topical medicines cause itchy, sharply bordered eczema.
DVT causes swollen, tender calf with warmth: Wells score and D-dimer.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: Compare the photos below. Venous eczema is scaly and itchy on **both** legs. Lipodermatosclerosis is indurated and tapering. True cellulitis is hot, tender, **one-sided** and expanding.

sub: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, crepitus: emergency surgery.

ddx.name: Venous eczema / stasis dermatitis
ddx.f: Bilateral or chronic, itchy, scale, haemosiderin, no fever

ddx.name: Acute lipodermatosclerosis
ddx.f: Painful, woody, red skin above the ankle, often misdiagnosed as cellulitis

ddx.name: DVT
ddx.f: Calf pain and swelling, less intense redness

ddx.name: Contact dermatitis (e.g. to dressings)
ddx.f: Itchy, vesicular, matches the area covered

ddx.name: Necrotising fasciitis
ddx.f: **Severe pain out of proportion**, rapid progression, systemic toxicity. **ED**

ddx.name: Pyoderma gangrenosum / vasculitis
ddx.f: Ulcer edge features, purpura, systemic disease

refer.t: Pain out of proportion, purple bullae, crepitus, or a rapidly spreading area: **necrotising fasciitis**.
Sepsis signs: low blood pressure, tachycardia, confusion, mottling.
A cold, pulseless or ischaemic limb.
A diabetic foot that is hot, red or ulcerated.

ul: Unnecessary antibiotics and admissions; missed DVT or necrotising infection.
Depends on cause; stasis dermatitis is chronic and needs compression.

pearls: Venous eczema responds to emollient plus a topical steroid and compression (after ABPI). Antibiotics do nothing for it.
Recurrent ‘cellulitis’ in the same leg may be lipodermatosclerosis. Look at the whole leg history.

quiz.q: When should you think of Red leg: differentials & referral?
quiz.a: Any patient presenting with ‘cellulitis’, especially if both legs are involved, it is chronic or itchy, or there is no fever.
Most bilateral red legs are venous (stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis) or oedema, not infection.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Ask: one leg or two, acute or chronic, fever or not, itch or pain? Treat the actual cause.
Necrotising fasciitis, sepsis, DVT, critical ischaemia and diabetic foot infection.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Pain out of proportion, purple bullae, crepitus, or a rapidly spreading area: **necrotising fasciitis**.
